misfits.thing: Asphalt road surface
misfits.where: Center and foreground of the image, running up the middle of the village street
misfits.why: Dark, smooth tarmac is a modern paving material. A village around 1350 would have had dirt, gravel, or cobbled streets.

misfits.thing: White dashed lane markings
misfits.where: Center of the road, from the foreground toward the distant village
misfits.why: Painted lane-divider lines are a modern traffic convention that did not exist in medieval Europe.

misfits.thing: Asphalt road surface
misfits.where: Center and right of the image, the road running through the village
misfits.why: Smooth dark paved asphalt is a modern road surface; around 1350 village streets were unpaved dirt or packed earth.

misfits.thing: White painted dashed center and edge lane markings
misfits.where: Down the middle of the road and along the right edge in the foreground
misfits.why: Painted traffic lane markings are a modern road feature and did not exist in medieval Bohemia.

misfits.thing: Asphalt road with white dashed lane markings
misfits.where: Center and right foreground, running up the middle of the street
misfits.why: Paved asphalt with painted dashed lane lines is a modern road feature, not a 14th-century village lane of packed earth or cobbles.

misfits.thing: Red brick chimney stacks
misfits.where: Top left above the nearest thatched roof, and on the right-hand house roofline
misfits.why: The regular red brick chimneys are a later construction style; the thatched cottages of the period would have had simpler or no brick chimneys.

misfits.thing: Paved asphalt road surface
misfits.where: Center and right foreground, running from the bottom edge of the image up toward the village
misfits.why: Smooth dark asphalt is a modern paving material. A village street around 1350 would be dirt, mud, or cobbles.

misfits.thing: White dashed lane markings
misfits.where: Down the middle of the road, from the foreground to the background
misfits.why: Painted traffic lane lines belong to the automobile era and did not exist in medieval Bohemia.

misfits.thing: Asphalt road surface
misfits.where: Center and foreground of the image, running from the bottom edge up to the village in the distance
misfits.why: Smooth dark asphalt is a modern paving material; around 1350 village streets would be dirt, mud, or cobbled.

misfits.thing: White painted lane markings (dashed center line and solid edge line)
misfits.where: Down the middle of the road in the foreground and midground, including the long solid stripe at lower center
misfits.why: Painted traffic lane lines are a modern road feature and did not exist in medieval Bohemia.

misfits.thing: Asphalt road with white dashed center lane markings
misfits.where: Occupies the right half of the image, running down the middle of the village street from the foreground to the distance
misfits.why: Paved asphalt with painted lane lines is a modern road surface. Around 1350 village streets were dirt or packed earth, not paved and striped.

misfits.thing: Chimney stack on the right cottage
misfits.where: Top right corner, rising from the thatched roof of the right-hand house
misfits.why: The orange brick chimney looks more like a later-medieval or early-modern feature. Rural peasant cottages around 1350 usually had a central hearth with a smoke hole rather than a brick chimney.

misfits.thing: Brick or stone chimney with smoke rising from a thatched cottage roof
misfits.where: Upper right, on the thatched roof of the cottage at the right edge, behind the woman in the red dress
misfits.why: Chimneys like this were rare on 14th-century peasant houses, which typically vented smoke through the roof or a smoke hole rather than a built chimney stack.

misfits.thing: Street lamp with a metal pole and dome-shaped electric-style lamp housing with a glowing bulb
misfits.where: Right side of the image, on the sidewalk curb beside the shop entrance, rising above the amphora
misfits.why: Electric-style street lighting with a metal fixture and bulb is a modern invention and does not belong on a 1st-century AD Roman street, which would have been lit by oil lamps or torches.

misfits.thing: Tall grey metal street lamppost with a modern-looking enclosed lamp head
misfits.where: Right side of the image, rising from the sidewalk edge beside the shop front to the top right corner, with its glowing lamp near the top
misfits.why: Its smooth industrial metal pole and enclosed lamp fixture look like a modern streetlight. Roman streets of the 1st century AD were lit by oil lamps or torches, not metal electric-style lamp posts.

misfits.thing: Black metal street lamp with a glowing enclosed bulb
misfits.where: Right side of the image, on a tall dark pole rising from the sidewalk beside the shop front, with its lamp head near the top right
misfits.why: Its cast-metal pole and glass-enclosed electric-style bulb look modern. In 1st-century Rome, streets were lit by oil lamps or torches, not fixtures like this.

misfits.thing: Modern metal street lamp with a glowing enclosed light head
misfits.where: Right side of the frame, on the sidewalk beside the pottery shop, rising to the top right edge
misfits.why: Its straight grey metal pole, cast base, and enclosed electric-style lamp fixture are modern. Roman streets of the 1st century AD were lit by oil lamps or torches, not fixtures like this.

misfits.thing: Black metal street lamp with a modern-style lamp head and glowing light fixture
misfits.where: Right side of the image, rising from the pavement beside the shop doorway and the amphora, extending up past the upper floor
misfits.why: Its sleek industrial design and electric-style light fixture do not match 1st-century AD Roman street furniture, which relied on oil lamps or torches.

misfits.thing: Metal street lamp with a dome shade and electric-style bulb
misfits.where: Right side of the street, rising from the sidewalk edge beside the shop front to the top of the frame
misfits.why: Its tall dark metal post, dome-shaped fixture and bright bulb look modern. Romans had no street lighting like this and relied on hand-held torches or oil lamps.

misfits.thing: Ornate scrolled wrought-iron lantern bracket
misfits.where: Upper left, mounted on the wall above the shop awning (roughly x 65-295, y 195-420)
misfits.why: Its elaborate curling scrollwork resembles Victorian or medieval ironwork more than the simpler Roman metal fittings of the 1st century AD.

misfits.thing: Ornate scrolled wrought-iron bracket with chain holding the hanging oil lamp
misfits.where: Upper right, on the wall beside the shop entrance
misfits.why: Its decorative scrollwork and curling iron form look more like medieval or later European ironwork than the plainer metal fittings typical of 1st-century Roman buildings.

misfits.thing: Wall-mounted hanging lantern with a glass enclosure on a scrolled wrought-iron bracket
misfits.where: Upper left of the image, mounted on the wall beside the shop doorway
misfits.why: The glass-chimney lantern on an ornate scrolled iron bracket looks more medieval or early modern than 1st-century Roman, when lamps were typically ceramic or bronze oil lamps.

misfits.thing: Multi-pane window with a wooden grid of mullions
misfits.where: Right wall, upper right of the room, showing the snowy landscape outside
misfits.why: Glazed or divided-pane windows were not available in a Viking longhouse around 900; openings were typically unglazed, covered with cloth or shutters, or left open.

misfits.thing: Multi-pane window with glazed panes
misfits.where: Right side of the back wall, above the seated family
misfits.why: Clear glass panes set in a framed grid were not used in Viking Age houses around 900, which had shuttered openings or smoke holes rather than glazed windows.

misfits.thing: Multi-pane window with a grid of glass-looking panes
misfits.where: Right side wall, behind the seated woman
misfits.why: Glazed windows with muntins were not used in a Viking-age longhouse around 900; openings were small and closed with wooden shutters or left open.

misfits.thing: Window with a white-framed grid of small glass panes
misfits.where: Center-right of the back wall, above the bench where the family sits
misfits.why: Clear multi-pane glazing in a white-painted modern-looking frame is anachronistic for a Viking-age longhouse around 900, which would have had at most small openings or shuttered holes rather than glass windows.

misfits.thing: Multi-pane glazed window with a grid of small glass panes and a framed sash
misfits.where: Right-center wall, between the two shields, around x 560-680 and y 540-840
misfits.why: Glass windows were not used in Viking-age longhouses around 900 AD. Such buildings had small openings closed with wooden shutters or hides, and smoke escaped through roof openings.

misfits.thing: Multi-pane window with a grid of small rectangular panes
misfits.where: Center-right wall, upper middle of the image (roughly x 565-700, y 590-910), behind the seated man
misfits.why: Glazed window panes divided by wooden mullions were not used in a Viking-age longhouse around 900; openings were typically unglazed, closed with shutters, or left as smoke holes.

misfits.thing: Striped geometric flatweave rug (kilim-style)
misfits.where: Bottom right foreground (roughly x 620-1088, y 1480-1936) and along the right edge near the bench
misfits.why: Patterned kilim-style flatweave rugs are associated with later or other regional traditions; Viking-age floors were more likely covered with animal hides and plain woven textiles.

misfits.thing: Knitting work in the woman's hands
misfits.where: Center-right, in the woman's lap and hands beside the bench
misfits.why: Viking-age Scandinavians made textiles by weaving and nålbinding (knotless needle-looping), not knitting with two needles, which did not reach Norse households around 900.

misfits.thing: Glazed skylight with a rectangular frame, showing blue sky
misfits.where: Top center of the roof, above the smoke
misfits.why: Viking-age longhouses had smoke holes or wooden vents, not glass skylights with framed panes, which are a later construction feature.

misfits.thing: Striped, patterned flatweave rugs on the floor
misfits.where: Across the floor in the foreground, middle, and bottom left
misfits.why: Their bold banded kilim-style patterns resemble later Middle Eastern or Central Asian rugs more than the plain textiles and furs typical of a c. 900 Norse longhouse, though trade textiles were not impossible.

misfits.thing: Blue plastic bucket with a molded handle
misfits.where: Right of center, beside the man's legs, around the middle-right of the image
misfits.why: Molded plastic buckets like this are a modern material and design. An 1850s farmyard would use wooden, metal, or woven containers.

misfits.thing: Bright blue bucket with a wire handle
misfits.where: Held in the man's right hand, at the right side of the image beside his leg
misfits.why: Its glossy, uniformly colored finish looks like modern molded plastic, which was not available in the 1850s. Period buckets would be wood, tin, or galvanized metal with a dull finish.

misfits.thing: Blue plastic bucket with a wire handle
misfits.where: Right side of the image, held in the farmer's right hand near his hip
misfits.why: Its bright blue molded-plastic look and modern bucket shape do not fit an 1850s farmyard, when buckets would have been wood, metal, or leather.

misfits.thing: bright blue plastic bucket
misfits.where: right side of the yard, near the middle-right, beside the man's legs and the dirt ground
misfits.why: Brightly colored molded plastic was not available in the 1850s; a farmyard bucket of that period would be metal, wood, or leather.

misfits.thing: blue plastic bucket
misfits.where: lower left, beside the man's boots on the dirt ground
misfits.why: Its bright blue molded plastic form is a modern material and style. In the 1850s a farmyard bucket would have been wood, galvanized or tin metal, or woven material.

misfits.thing: Blue plastic bucket
misfits.where: Center-right of the dirt yard, to the right of the man and below the blue wagon
misfits.why: Its smooth molded plastic body and handle look modern. An 1850s farmyard would use wooden or metal buckets, like the wooden bucket the man is carrying.

misfits.thing: Yellow ear tag on the cow
misfits.where: On the cow's left ear, at the left edge of the image near the cow's head
misfits.why: Plastic livestock ear tags for identification came into common use in the 20th century, so they would not be expected on a cow in an 1850s farmyard.

misfits.thing: Black dome pendant lamp with a bare light bulb
misfits.where: Hanging from the ceiling at the top center of the room, above the central column
misfits.why: Its industrial-style metal shade and bulb suggest electric lighting, which does not fit a medieval scriptorium that would have been lit by candles, oil lamps, or daylight from the windows.

misfits.thing: Electric pendant ceiling lamp with a bare light bulb
misfits.where: Hanging from the ceiling at the top center of the room, above the middle of the scriptorium
misfits.why: The dark metal conical shade and exposed bulb look like modern electric lighting, which does not belong in a medieval monastery where the room would be lit by candles, oil lamps, or daylight.

misfits.thing: Hanging pendant lamp with a metal shade and a clear glass light bulb
misfits.where: Top center of the room, suspended from the wooden ceiling beams above the desks
misfits.why: The bulb and shade look like a modern electric light fixture, which does not fit a medieval monastery scriptorium that would have been lit by candles or oil lamps.

misfits.thing: Black metal pendant lamp with a glowing light bulb
misfits.where: Hanging from the ceiling at top center of the room
misfits.why: A bulb in a metal dome shade is an electric light fixture, which does not belong in a medieval monastery scriptorium that would have been lit by candles, oil lamps, or daylight.

misfits.thing: Shelved books with uniform colored spines
misfits.where: Bookcase on the left side of the room
misfits.why: The rows of neatly uniform, rectangular, colorful hardcover-style volumes look like modern printed books rather than hand-bound medieval codices with leather or wooden boards.

misfits.thing: Metal pendant lamp with an incandescent light bulb
misfits.where: Hanging from the ceiling at the top center of the room
misfits.why: Electric light fixtures did not exist in a medieval monastery; the scriptorium would have been lit by candles, oil lamps, or daylight.

misfits.thing: Electric light bulb with a metal dome shade hanging from the ceiling
misfits.where: Top center of the image, suspended from the wooden ceiling beams above the desks
misfits.why: A glass electric bulb and metal pendant lamp are anachronistic for a medieval monastery scriptorium, which would have been lit by candles, oil lamps, or daylight from the windows.

misfits.thing: Clear plastic water bottle with blue screw cap
misfits.where: Center-right of the forest floor, lying on its side among the autumn beech leaves
misfits.why: Man-made plastic litter does not belong on an undisturbed beech forest floor in a nature scene.

misfits.where: right side of the image, lying on the leaf litter near the middle-right ground

misfits.where: center-right foreground, lying on the leaf litter beside the mushroom cluster

misfits.thing: Clear plastic water bottle with blue screw cap
misfits.where: Center-right foreground, lying on the leaf litter between the mushroom cluster and the bottom-right leaves
misfits.why: Man-made plastic litter does not belong on a natural undisturbed beech forest floor.

misfits.thing: clear plastic water bottle with blue screw cap
misfits.where: center-right foreground, lying on the leaf litter below the mossy trunk and right of the mushroom cluster
misfits.why: Man-made plastic litter does not belong on a natural undisturbed beech forest floor.

misfits.thing: clear plastic water bottle with blue screw cap
misfits.where: lower right of the image, lying on the leaf litter in the foreground
misfits.why: Man-made plastic litter does not belong on a natural autumn beech forest floor.

misfits.thing: pine cone
misfits.where: center-right of the foreground, on the leaf litter beside the mushroom cluster and the moss-covered root
misfits.why: Pine cones come from conifers, but the scene is a pure beech forest with no conifers visible, so it is a natural item out of place for this setting.

misfits.thing: pine cone
misfits.where: right-center of the foreground, on the leaf litter beside the mossy tree base
misfits.why: A conifer cone is atypical for a pure beech forest floor, where the litter is beech leaves and the trees are all broadleaf beeches, so it suggests a nearby pine rather than this setting.

misfits.thing: Pine cone
misfits.where: Right side of the image, on the leaf litter near the mushroom cluster
misfits.why: It is a conifer cone, but the setting is a pure beech forest floor where conifer litter would not normally appear. It is natural debris, not man-made, so it is a mild botanical mismatch rather than a clear anachronism.

misfits.thing: High-voltage electricity pylon with power lines
misfits.where: Right side of the image, rising from the meadow near the cows and extending above the top edge
misfits.why: A large industrial steel lattice tower and its wires are man-made infrastructure that dominates and intrudes on an otherwise pastoral alpine nature scene.

misfits.thing: Steel electricity transmission pylon with power lines
misfits.where: Right of center, rising above the meadow and against the mountains and sky
misfits.why: A man-made utility structure of the kind found in a pristine alpine meadow. It is present-day technology, not a period error, but it is an industrial intrusion into an otherwise natural scene.

misfits.thing: Blue corrugated metal roof
misfits.where: Top right, covering the mud-brick storehouse behind the quay
misfits.why: Corrugated sheet metal is a modern roofing material. Ancient Egyptian storehouses had flat or vaulted mud-brick roofs, not ribbed metal sheeting.

misfits.thing: Corrugated grey metal-looking roof on the warehouse
misfits.where: Top right, covering the storehouse building along the quay
misfits.why: Its ridged, sheet-like finish resembles corrugated iron or modern metal roofing, which is anachronistic for c. 1400 BC Egypt, where flat mud-brick or timber roofs were typical.

misfits.thing: Corrugated sheet-metal roof
misfits.where: Top of the warehouse building on the right side of the image
misfits.why: Corrugated metal roofing is a modern material. Ancient Egyptian buildings of about 1400 BC had flat or mud-brick roofs, not ribbed metal sheeting.

misfits.thing: Corrugated metal roof sheets on the storehouse
misfits.where: Top of the mud-brick storehouse, upper center-right of the image
misfits.why: Corrugated galvanized metal roofing is a modern material; ancient Egyptian storehouses would have had flat mud-brick or palm-wood and reed roofs.

misfits.thing: Metal chain linking the mooring posts
misfits.where: Between the wooden bollards along the quay edge, visible above the lower reed boat (around the center and lower-center of the image)
misfits.why: Iron chain was not used for mooring around 1400 BC; boats would have been secured with rope, plaited papyrus or reed cordage.

misfits.thing: Corrugated metal roof sheeting on the warehouse
misfits.where: Top of the mud-brick storehouse, spanning roughly the upper middle and right of the image
misfits.why: Corrugated sheet metal is a modern material and form. Around 1400 BC the roof would have been flat or pitched with palm-log beams and reed or mud-plastered thatch, not ribbed metal.

misfits.thing: Stacked burlap-style sacks of coarse woven fiber
misfits.where: Right side beside the warehouse entrance, and in the foreground reed boat
misfits.why: The sacks have a coarse, jute- or burlap-like weave and rough texture that resembles modern grain or sand bags. Egyptian goods were more often stored in clay jars, baskets or linen-wrapped bundles, so this sack style looks anachronistic.

misfits.thing: Corrugated metal roof on the mudbrick storehouse
misfits.where: Top of the large building on the right, covering the whole structure
misfits.why: Corrugated sheet metal is a modern material and did not exist in ancient Egypt around 1400 BC, which used mud-brick with flat or wood-and-reed roofs.

misfits.thing: Chain links connecting boats to the mooring posts
misfits.where: Between the wooden posts and the reed boats, in the lower center and on the left side of the quay edge
misfits.why: The links look like metal chains, while Bronze Age Egyptians secured boats with rope, not chain.

misfits.thing: Stone temple with pylon architecture on the far bank
misfits.where: Distant left-center background, across the river beyond the palm groves
misfits.why: The temple's form resembles a later Ptolemaic-era temple complex, which was built around 1,000 years after 1400 BC.
